newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia cattle slaughter rises sharply.
newsitem.headline: Australia cattle slaughter rises sharply.

text.p: Australian cattle slaughter statistics provide an indication of the hardships being endured by producers, particularly southern Australia, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said on Tuesday.

In the states of New South Wales and Victoria, slaughters in the year to April rose by 4.6 percent and 9.3 percent respectively, driven primarily by female kills, the AMLC said in its Meat and Livestock Review. "These have exceeded year-ago levels by 6.4 percent in New South Wales and a massive 37 percent in Victoria, the peak meat marketing authority said.
In Queensland, slaughter rates have also gathered pace.

In the first four months of 1997, weekly throughput in Queensland was around 5,000 head above the 1996 weekly average, the AMLC said. However, since April, numbers have increased to the point where around 8,000 head more are being killed each week compared to the same periods a year ago, it said.
Australian slaughter rates are now 7.9 percent above the same period in 1996, the AMLC said.

"These large slaughter levels have been sustained in the face of a large exodus of cattle to the live export trade, which has affected cattle availability in the north and a lesser extent in the south," the AMLC said.
Lower carcass weights have restricted the rise in production to around 6.4 percent above last year, it said.
Exports were strong in May, buoyed by recent high production levels, the AMLC said.
Beef and veal exports in the first five months of 1997 ran 7.6 percent above the comparable 1996 level, the AMLC said.
Higher export volumes have been largely confined to shipments of frozen product to manufacturing beef markets, the AMLC said.
Combined volumes from January to May to the U.S., Canada, Taiwan and Indonesia have increased by 45 percent on last year, the AMLC said.
Poor market conditions in north Asia, though, have seen exports to Japan fall 1.5 percent and to Korea decline 20 percent on 1996, it said.
A five percent fall in chilled beef sales to Japan was behind the decline in exports to Japan, the AMLC said.
